newsitem.title: USA: Ill. governor set to sign airport takeover bill.
newsitem.headline: Ill. governor set to sign airport takeover bill.

text.p: Illinois Gov. Jim Edgar will sign into law a bill allowing the state to take over a small airport in Chicago, the governor's spokesman said Thursday.
But that signing will be delayed for a while in the hope Chicago Mayor Richard Daley will decide to compromise on the use of Meigs Field, said Eric Robinson, the spokesman.

Daley, who held a news conference Wednesday blasting the passage of the bill by the Illinois House Tuesday night, made it clear that a compromise was not in the cards. The bill was subsequently passed by the Senate in a 32 to 27 vote Wednesday night.

The mayor wants to turn the airport on the city's downtown lakefront into a $27 million, bond-financed nature park. Edgar wants to keep Meigs Field operating as a airport for corporate aircraft and other users. So far lawsuits filed by the Edgar Administration in both state and federal courts have been decided in the city's favor.

At Wednesday's news conference, Daley argued that a park and and an airport are not compatible and he said if the state takes over Meigs Field, Illinois taxpayers would face paying $4 million for operating the airfield, as well as $30 million or more in capital expenses. The city shuttered the airport earlier this fall.

Even if Edgar signs the bill into law it will not take effect until June 1 because its passage lacked a required three-fifths vote for immediate effect. All bills passed during the fall veto session must have super-majority approval to become effective immediately, under state statutes.

However, there is a possibility that the Republican-controlled legislature may vote again on the bill in January, shortly before a new legislature is sworn in and Republicans lose control of the House as a result of the November 5 election.

Patty Schuh, spokeswoman for Senate President James "Pate" Philip, R-Wood Dale, said a simple majority vote at that time would give the bill immediate effect because the vote would come after the first of the year.

Meanwhile, the legislature's fall veto session is set to wind down Thursday. On Wednesday, opposition from House Democrats sunk a $610 million general obligation bonding bill. Robinson said Edgar believed it was "unfortunate that Democrats would not vote for important projects for schools and prisons."

Robinson also said the governor decided not to push for an advisory referendum on school funding during the session because lawmakers had assured him they would take action on the matter during the spring session.
